sections.title: Linear Algebra — Matrices
sections.summary: Types of matrices, operations, transpose, inverse, rank, trace.
sections.content:
## 1. Basics and special matrices

An $m\times n$ matrix has $m$ rows and $n$ columns. $A+B$ needs equal order. $AB$ is defined only when (columns of $A$) = (rows of $B$): $A_{m\times n}B_{n\times p}=C_{m\times p}$. In general $AB\ne BA$.

| Type | Condition |
|---|---|
| Symmetric | $A^T=A$ |
| Skew-symmetric | $A^T=-A$ (diagonal is all 0) |
| Orthogonal | $A^TA=AA^T=I$, so $A^{-1}=A^T$, $\det A=\pm1$ |
| Idempotent | $A^2=A$ |
| Involutory | $A^2=I$ |
| Nilpotent | $A^k=0$ for some $k$ |
| Diagonal / Triangular | non-diagonal / one side of the diagonal is 0 |
| Hermitian / Unitary | $A^H=A$ / $A^HA=I$ (complex analogues) |

Every square matrix splits uniquely as $A=\tfrac12(A+A^T)+\tfrac12(A-A^T)$ = symmetric + skew-symmetric.

## 2. Transpose, inverse and trace rules

$$(AB)^T=B^TA^T,\qquad (AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1},\qquad (A^T)^{-1}=(A^{-1})^T$$

$$\operatorname{tr}(A)=\sum a_{ii},\qquad \operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(A)=\sum\lambda_i$$

For any real $A$: $A^TA$ and $AA^T$ are symmetric, and so is $A+A^T$; $A-A^T$ is skew-symmetric.

## 3. Inverse

$A^{-1}=\dfrac{\operatorname{adj}(A)}{\det A}$ exists iff $\det A\neq0$ (non-singular). For $2\times2$:

$$\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}^{-1}=\frac1{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}$$

Gauss–Jordan method: row-reduce $[A\,|\,I]$ to $[I\,|\,A^{-1}]$.

## 4. Rank

Rank = number of non-zero rows in row-echelon form = number of linearly independent rows = number of independent columns.

- $\operatorname{rank}(A)\le\min(m,n)$, $\operatorname{rank}(A)=\operatorname{rank}(A^T)$
- $\operatorname{rank}(AB)\le\min(\operatorname{rank}A,\operatorname{rank}B)$
- Row operations do not change rank
- Full rank square matrix $\iff$ invertible $\iff\det\ne0$
- Rank–nullity: $\operatorname{rank}(A)+\operatorname{nullity}(A)=n$ (number of columns)
- Idempotent matrix: $\operatorname{rank}=\operatorname{trace}$
- A nilpotent $n\times n$ matrix with $A^2=0$ has $\operatorname{rank}\le n/2$

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Rank nikalne ke liye hamesha row-echelon form banao. Order wale sawaal me pehle dekho ki product defined hai ya nahi.
keyPoints: Rank–nullity: rank + nullity = number of columns

sections.title: Linear Algebra — Determinants
sections.summary: Properties, cofactor expansion, adjoint, special determinants.
sections.content:
## 1. Computing a determinant

- $2\times2$: $\begin{vmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc$
- $3\times3$: expand along any row/column using cofactors $C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$: $\det A=\sum_j a_{ij}C_{ij}$
- Triangular (or diagonal) matrix: $\det$ = product of diagonal entries
- Gaussian elimination to triangular form: $O(n^3)$ (cofactor expansion is $O(n!)$)

## 2. Properties (most tested)

| Operation | Effect on $\det$ |
|---|---|
| Swap two rows/columns | sign changes |
| Multiply one row by $k$ | $\det$ multiplied by $k$ |
| Add multiple of one row to another | unchanged |
| Two equal / proportional rows | $\det=0$ |
| Zero row or column | $\det=0$ |

$$\det(AB)=\det A\det B,\quad \det A^T=\det A,\quad \det(kA)=k^n\det A,\quad \det(A^{-1})=\frac1{\det A}$$

- Skew-symmetric matrix of **odd** order: $\det=0$
- Orthogonal: $\det=\pm1$; nilpotent: $\det=0$; idempotent: $\det\in\{0,1\}$
- $\det A=\prod\lambda_i$ (product of eigenvalues)
- Block triangular: $\det\begin{bmatrix}P&Q\\0&R\end{bmatrix}=\det P\det R$

## 3. Adjoint

$$A\,\operatorname{adj}(A)=\operatorname{adj}(A)\,A=\det(A)\,I,\qquad \det(\operatorname{adj}A)=(\det A)^{n-1}$$

$$\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)=(\det A)^{n-2}A,\qquad \det(\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A))=(\det A)^{(n-1)^2}$$

## 4. Special determinants

- Vandermonde: $\begin{vmatrix}1&x_1&x_1^2\\1&x_2&x_2^2\\1&x_3&x_3^2\end{vmatrix}=(x_2-x_1)(x_3-x_1)(x_3-x_2)$
- Circulant $\begin{vmatrix}a&b&c\\b&c&a\\c&a&b\end{vmatrix}=-(a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc)$, which is 0 when $a+b+c=0$
- Cramer's rule: for $Ax=b$ with $\det A\ne0$, $x_i=\det A_i/\det A$ ($A_i$ = $A$ with column $i$ replaced by $b$)

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Scalar multiple me $k^n$ aata hai, sirf $k$ nahi. Adjoint wale sawaal me hamesha $n$ ki value dhyan se lo.
keyPoints: Row swap flips the sign; row replacement keeps $\det$ unchanged

sections.title: Linear Algebra — Systems of Linear Equations
sections.summary: Consistency, rank test, homogeneous systems, null space, Gaussian elimination.
sections.content:
## 1. Setup

$Ax=b$ with $A$ of order $m\times n$ (m equations, n unknowns). The augmented matrix is $[A\,|\,b]$.

## 2. Rouché–Capelli (rank) test

Let $r=\operatorname{rank}(A)$ and $r'=\operatorname{rank}[A\,|\,b]$.

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| $r\ne r'$ | inconsistent, **no solution** |
| $r=r'=n$ | **unique** solution |
| $r=r'<n$ | **infinitely many** solutions, with $n-r$ free variables |

A linear system over $\mathbb R$ never has exactly 2 (or any finite number $>1$) of solutions.

## 3. Homogeneous system $Ax=0$

- Always consistent (trivial solution $x=0$).
- Non-trivial solution exists iff $\operatorname{rank}(A)<n$. For square $A$: iff $\det A=0$.
- If $m<n$ (fewer equations than unknowns), a non-trivial solution always exists.
- Solutions form a subspace (null space) of dimension $n-\operatorname{rank}(A)$.
- Solution of $Ax=b$ = particular solution + any vector of the null space.

## 4. Vector space facts

- Vectors $v_1,\dots,v_k$ are independent iff the matrix with these as columns has rank $k$.
- $Ax=b$ is solvable for **every** $b$ iff $\operatorname{rank}(A)=m$ (full row rank).
- For square $A$: unique solution for every $b$ iff $\det A\ne0$.
- Dimension of column space = dimension of row space = rank.

## 5. Methods

- **Gaussian elimination**: reduce to row echelon form, back-substitute. Cost $\approx n^3/3$ multiplications.
- **Gauss–Jordan**: reduce to reduced row echelon form, about $n^3/2$ operations.
- **Cramer's rule**: for square non-singular systems; practical only for small $n$.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Parameter wale sawaal me augmented matrix ko echelon form me laao, phir last row se rank compare karo: $0=\text{non-zero}$ aaye to inconsistent.
keyPoints: Unique iff rank $=n$; infinite iff rank $<n$ (free variables $=n-r$)
Homogeneous system with $m<n$ always has a non-trivial solution
A linear system has 0, 1 or infinitely many solutions, never exactly 2

sections.title: Linear Algebra — Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
sections.content:
## 1. Definition

$Av=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$. Eigenvalues are roots of the characteristic equation $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. For $2\times2$: $\lambda^2-\operatorname{tr}(A)\lambda+\det(A)=0$.

For eigenvalue $\lambda$, eigenvectors are the non-zero solutions of $(A-\lambda I)v=0$.

## 2. Key properties

- $\sum\lambda_i=\operatorname{tr}(A)$, $\prod\lambda_i=\det(A)$
- $A$ is singular iff 0 is an eigenvalue
- Eigenvalues of: $A^k\to\lambda^k$, $A^{-1}\to1/\lambda$, $A+cI\to\lambda+c$, $cA\to c\lambda$, $p(A)\to p(\lambda)$, $A^T\to$ same as $A$
- Triangular / diagonal matrix: eigenvalues are the diagonal entries
- $AB$ and $BA$ have the same non-zero eigenvalues
- Eigenvectors for **distinct** eigenvalues are linearly independent

| Matrix type | Eigenvalues |
|---|---|
| Real symmetric | all real |
| Real skew-symmetric | purely imaginary or 0 |
| Orthogonal / Unitary | $|\lambda|=1$ |
| Idempotent ($A^2=A$) | 0 or 1 |
| Involutory ($A^2=I$) | $\pm1$ |
| Nilpotent | 0 |
| Positive definite | all $>0$ |

## 3. Cayley–Hamilton theorem

Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation: if $p(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda I)$ then $p(A)=0$. It gives $A^{-1}$ and higher powers without computing them directly. Example: $A^2-5A+6I=0\Rightarrow A^{-1}=\frac{5I-A}{6}$.

## 4. Diagonalization

- Algebraic multiplicity (AM) = multiplicity of $\lambda$ as a root. Geometric multiplicity (GM) = $\dim\ker(A-\lambda I)$. Always $1\le GM\le AM$.
- $A$ is diagonalizable iff $GM=AM$ for every eigenvalue (iff $n$ independent eigenvectors). Distinct eigenvalues guarantee this.
- Then $A=PDP^{-1}$ and $A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$.
- Real symmetric matrices are always **orthogonally** diagonalizable ($A=QDQ^T$).
- Example of a non-diagonalizable matrix: $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ (AM = 2, GM = 1).

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Sawaal me poori matrix nahi maangte to trace aur determinant se kaam chalao. $f(A)$ ke eigenvalues $f(\lambda)$ hote hain.
keyPoints: Diagonalizable iff GM = AM for all eigenvalues
Real symmetric: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors

sections.title: Linear Algebra — LU Decomposition
sections.summary: Doolittle/Crout, pivoting, solving systems, determinant from U, complexity.
sections.content:
## 1. Idea

Factor a square matrix as $A=LU$ where $L$ is lower triangular and $U$ is upper triangular. This is Gaussian elimination recorded as a matrix product.

- **Doolittle**: $L$ has 1s on the diagonal.
- **Crout**: $U$ has 1s on the diagonal.
- **Cholesky**: $A=LL^T$ for symmetric positive definite $A$.
- $A=LDU$ with unit-diagonal $L,U$ and diagonal $D$.

## 2. Existence

- $A=LU$ without row exchanges exists if all **leading principal minors** are non-zero (then it is unique for unit-diagonal $L$).
- If a pivot becomes 0, row exchanges are needed: $PA=LU$ ($P$ = permutation matrix). This exists for every non-singular matrix.
- Example needing pivoting: $\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ (first pivot is 0).

## 3. Worked example

$$A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1&1\\4&3&3\\8&7&9\end{bmatrix}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\4&3&1\end{bmatrix}}_{L}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}2&1&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix}}_{U}$$

Multipliers: $l_{21}=4/2=2$, $l_{31}=8/2=4$; after step 1 the second column pivot is 1, so $l_{32}=3/1=3$.

## 4. Using LU

- Solve $Ax=b$: solve $Ly=b$ by **forward substitution**, then $Ux=y$ by **back substitution**; each is $O(n^2)$.
- Factorization costs $\approx\tfrac13n^3$ multiplications ($\tfrac23n^3$ flops), i.e. $O(n^3)$. Factor once, solve many right-hand sides cheaply.
- $\det A=\prod u_{ii}$ (Doolittle, no pivoting). With pivoting multiply by $(-1)^{\text{number of swaps}}$.
- Inverse can be found by solving $n$ systems $Ax_i=e_i$.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** U ka diagonal product = determinant. L ke neeche ke entries wahi multipliers hain jo elimination me use hue.
keyPoints: Exists without pivoting if all leading principal minors $\ne0$

sections.title: Calculus — Limits
sections.summary: Standard limits, indeterminate forms, L'Hôpital, series expansions, growth rates.
sections.content:
## 1. Basics

$\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ exists iff the left-hand limit and right-hand limit both exist and are equal. Limit laws: sum, product, quotient (denominator limit $\ne0$), composition.

**Squeeze theorem:** if $g(x)\le f(x)\le h(x)$ near $a$ and $g,h\to L$, then $f\to L$.

## 2. Standard limits (memorize)

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}$, $\frac{\tan x}{x}$, $\frac{\sin^{-1}x}{x}$ | $1$ |
| $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}$ | $\tfrac12$ |
| $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-1}{x}$, $\ \frac{\ln(1+x)}{x}$ | $1$ |
| $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{a^x-1}{x}$ | $\ln a$ |
| $\lim_{x\to a}\frac{x^n-a^n}{x-a}$ | $n\,a^{n-1}$ |
| $\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\frac1x\right)^x$, $\ \lim_{x\to0}(1+x)^{1/x}$ | $e$ |
| $\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\frac ax\right)^x$ | $e^a$ |
| $\lim_{x\to0^+}x\ln x$ | $0$ |

## 3. Indeterminate forms and L'Hôpital's rule

Indeterminate: $\frac00,\ \frac\infty\infty,\ 0\cdot\infty,\ \infty-\infty,\ 1^\infty,\ 0^0,\ \infty^0$.

**L'Hôpital:** if $\frac{f}{g}$ is $\frac00$ or $\frac\infty\infty$ at $a$ and $\lim\frac{f'}{g'}$ exists, then $\lim\frac fg=\lim\frac{f'}{g'}$ (repeat if needed). For $1^\infty$, $0^0$, $\infty^0$ take $\ln$ first: $\lim f^g=e^{\lim g\ln f}$.

## 4. Series (fastest way for $0/0$ limits)

$$\sin x=x-\tfrac{x^3}{6}+\dots,\quad \cos x=1-\tfrac{x^2}{2}+\tfrac{x^4}{24}-\dots,\quad e^x=1+x+\tfrac{x^2}{2}+\dots,\quad \ln(1+x)=x-\tfrac{x^2}{2}+\dots$$

## 5. Limits at infinity and growth order

- Rational function $\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$ as $x\to\infty$: compare degrees. Equal degrees → ratio of leading coefficients; deg P < deg Q → 0; deg P > deg Q → $\pm\infty$.
- Growth: $\ln x\ll x^a\ll e^x\ll x!\ll x^x$ as $x\to\infty$ (this order is also used in algorithm analysis).
- $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{|x|}{x}$ does **not** exist (left $=-1$, right $=+1$).

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** $0/0$ me L'Hôpital ya Taylor series use karo; $1^\infty$ me $e^{\lim g(f-1)}$ shortcut lagao.
keyPoints: Growth: $\ln x\ll x^a\ll e^x\ll x!\ll x^x$
Limit exists iff left limit = right limit

sections.title: Calculus — Continuity and Differentiability
sections.summary: Continuity, types of discontinuity, differentiability, differentiation rules.
sections.content:
## 1. Continuity

$f$ is continuous at $a$ iff $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=f(a)$.

Types of discontinuity:
- **Removable**: limit exists but $\ne f(a)$ or $f(a)$ undefined (e.g. $\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}$ at 1)
- **Jump**: left and right limits exist but differ (e.g. $\lfloor x\rfloor$)
- **Infinite**: limit is $\pm\infty$ (e.g. $1/x$ at 0)
- **Oscillatory**: no limit (e.g. $\sin(1/x)$ at 0)

Sums, products, compositions of continuous functions are continuous; polynomials, $e^x$, $\sin x$, $\cos x$ are continuous everywhere.

**On a closed interval $[a,b]$**, a continuous $f$ is bounded, attains its maximum and minimum (Extreme Value Theorem) and takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ (Intermediate Value Theorem).

## 2. Differentiability

$f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$ exists iff left derivative = right derivative.

- Differentiable $\Rightarrow$ continuous. **Converse is false**: $|x|$ is continuous at 0 but not differentiable.
- Non-differentiable points: corners ($|x|$), cusps ($x^{2/3}$), vertical tangents ($x^{1/3}$), discontinuities.
- $f(x)=x\sin\frac1x$ ($f(0)=0$): continuous at 0, not differentiable. $f(x)=x^2\sin\frac1x$: differentiable at 0 with $f'(0)=0$ but $f'$ is not continuous at 0.
- $f(x)=x|x|$ is differentiable at 0 ($f'(0)=0$) but not twice differentiable.
- $f(x)=|x-1|+|x-2|$ is not differentiable at exactly $x=1$ and $x=2$.

## 3. Piecewise functions

For $f=g(x)$ on $x\le a$ and $h(x)$ on $x>a$: continuity needs $g(a)=h(a)$; differentiability additionally needs $g'(a)=h'(a)$.

## 4. Differentiation rules

$(uv)'=u'v+uv'$, $\left(\frac uv\right)'=\frac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, chain rule $(f\circ g)'=f'(g)g'$.

| $f$ | $f'$ |
|---|---|
| $x^n$ | $nx^{n-1}$ |
| $e^x$, $a^x$ | $e^x$, $a^x\ln a$ |
| $\ln x$ | $1/x$ |
| $\sin x$, $\cos x$, $\tan x$ | $\cos x$, $-\sin x$, $\sec^2x$ |
| $\sin^{-1}x$, $\tan^{-1}x$ | $\frac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$, $\frac1{1+x^2}$ |
| $x^x$ | $x^x(1+\ln x)$ (logarithmic differentiation) |

Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides w.r.t. $x$. For $x^2+y^2=r^2$: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac xy$.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Piecewise function me pehle continuity ka equation likho, phir derivative barabar karo. Do unknown = do equations.
keyPoints: Continuous on $[a,b]$ $\Rightarrow$ bounded, attains max/min, IVT holds
Four discontinuity types: removable, jump, infinite, oscillatory

sections.title: Calculus — Maxima and Minima
sections.summary: Critical points, first and second derivative tests, global extrema, two-variable case.
sections.content:
## 1. Single variable

**Critical points:** $f'(c)=0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist.

**First derivative test:** $f'$ changes $+\to-$ at $c$: local max; $-\to+$: local min; no sign change: neither.

**Second derivative test** (when $f'(c)=0$): $f''(c)>0$ local min; $f''(c)<0$ local max; $f''(c)=0$ inconclusive (use the first derivative test or higher derivatives).

**Point of inflection:** concavity changes, $f''(c)=0$ (e.g. $x^3$ at 0).

**Global extrema on $[a,b]$:** evaluate $f$ at all critical points inside $(a,b)$ and at the endpoints; compare. (Guaranteed to exist for continuous $f$.)

## 2. Useful quick results

- $ax^2+bx+c$ ($a>0$): minimum $c-\frac{b^2}{4a}$ at $x=-\frac b{2a}$
- $a\sin x+b\cos x$ has range $[-\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\sqrt{a^2+b^2}]$
- AM–GM: $x+\frac kx\ge2\sqrt k$ for $x>0$, equality at $x=\sqrt k$
- Rectangle with fixed perimeter: max area is a square
- $f(x)=xe^{-x}$: maximum at $x=1$
- $f(x)=x^4-4x^3$: $f'=4x^2(x-3)$, so $x=3$ is a minimum but $x=0$ is **not** an extremum (no sign change)

## 3. Two variables $f(x,y)$

Stationary point: $f_x=f_y=0$. Let $D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2$.

| Condition | Nature |
|---|---|
| $D>0,\ f_{xx}>0$ | local minimum |
| $D>0,\ f_{xx}<0$ | local maximum |
| $D<0$ | saddle point |
| $D=0$ | inconclusive |

Example: $f=x^2-y^2$ has a saddle at the origin; $f=x^2+y^2-2x-4y+7=(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2+2$ has minimum value 2 at $(1,2)$.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Closed interval me hamesha endpoints bhi check karo. $f''=0$ aaye to second derivative test fail ho jata hai.
keyPoints: Closed interval: compare critical points and endpoints

sections.title: Calculus — Mean Value Theorem
sections.summary: Rolle, Lagrange, Cauchy, IVT, applications and Taylor's theorem.
sections.content:
## 1. Rolle's theorem

If $f$ is (i) continuous on $[a,b]$, (ii) differentiable on $(a,b)$, (iii) $f(a)=f(b)$, then there is $c\in(a,b)$ with $f'(c)=0$.

*Consequence:* between two real roots of $f$ there is a root of $f'$. A polynomial of degree $n$ with $n$ distinct real roots has $n-1$ real roots of $f'$.

## 2. Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem (LMVT)

If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, there exists $c\in(a,b)$ with

$$f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$$

(Geometrically: some tangent is parallel to the chord.) Rolle is the special case $f(a)=f(b)$.

Examples: $f=x^2$ on $[1,3]$ gives $c=2$. $f=x^3$ on $[0,2]$: $3c^2=4\Rightarrow c=\frac2{\sqrt3}\approx1.1547$.

## 3. Cauchy's MVT

If $f,g$ are continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$ and $g'\ne0$: $\ \dfrac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{g(b)-g(a)}$.

## 4. Applications

- $f'(x)=0$ on an interval $\Rightarrow f$ is constant; $f'>0\Rightarrow$ strictly increasing.
- Bounds: if $|f'(x)|\le M$ then $|f(b)-f(a)|\le M|b-a|$ (e.g. $|\sin a-\sin b|\le|a-b|$).
- Inequalities: $\ln(1+x)<x$ and $e^x>1+x$ for $x>0$.
- **Intermediate Value Theorem:** continuous $f$ on $[a,b]$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$. If $f(a)f(b)<0$ there is a root in $(a,b)$.

## 5. Taylor / Maclaurin (generalised MVT)

$$f(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)+\frac{f''(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2+\dots+\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n+R_n$$

**Conditions matter:** $f(x)=|x|$ on $[-1,1]$ has $f(-1)=f(1)$ but no point with $f'(c)=0$, because $f$ is not differentiable at 0.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Rolle ke liye teeno conditions chahiye. Derivative ka bound dekh kar function ki value ka upper bound nikalna MVT ka favourite sawaal hai.
keyPoints: Rolle implies $n$ distinct roots of $p$ give $n-1$ roots of $p'$
All hypotheses (continuity and differentiability) are necessary

sections.title: Calculus — Integration
sections.summary: Techniques, definite integral properties, improper integrals, Leibniz rule, Riemann sums.
sections.content:
## 1. Standard integrals

$\int x^ndx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$ ($n\ne-1$), $\int\frac{dx}x=\ln|x|$, $\int e^xdx=e^x$, $\int a^xdx=\frac{a^x}{\ln a}$, $\int\sin x=-\cos x$, $\int\cos x=\sin x$, $\int\sec^2x=\tan x$, $\int\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\tan^{-1}x$, $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}=\sin^{-1}x$.

## 2. Techniques

- **Substitution:** $\int f(g(x))g'(x)dx=\int f(u)du$
- **By parts:** $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$ (choose $u$ by ILATE: Inverse trig, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential). Example: $\int xe^xdx=(x-1)e^x$
- **Partial fractions** for rational functions
- $\int e^x(f(x)+f'(x))dx=e^xf(x)$

## 3. Definite integral properties

$$\int_a^bf=-\int_b^af,\qquad \int_a^bf(x)dx=\int_a^bf(a+b-x)dx$$

- Even $f$: $\int_{-a}^af=2\int_0^af$. Odd $f$: $\int_{-a}^af=0$.
- Periodic with period $T$: $\int_0^{nT}f=n\int_0^Tf$.
- $\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}dx=\frac\pi4$ (by the $a+b-x$ trick).
- $\int_a^b|f|$: split at the points where $f$ changes sign.

## 4. Wallis / Gamma results

$\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^nx\,dx$: $n=1:1,\ n=2:\frac\pi4,\ n=3:\frac23,\ n=4:\frac{3\pi}{16},\ n=5:\frac8{15}$.

$\int_0^\infty x^ne^{-x}dx=n!$ and $\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}dx=\frac{\sqrt\pi}2$.

## 5. Improper integrals

- $\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x^p}$ converges iff $p>1$ (value $\frac1{p-1}$).
- $\int_0^1\frac{dx}{x^p}$ converges iff $p<1$ (value $\frac1{1-p}$). So $\int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt x}=2$ but $\int_0^1\frac{dx}x$ diverges.

## 6. Other results

- **Fundamental theorem:** $\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^xf(t)dt=f(x)$.
- **Leibniz rule:** $\frac{d}{dx}\int_{a(x)}^{b(x)}f(t)dt=f(b(x))b'(x)-f(a(x))a'(x)$.
- **Average value** of $f$ on $[a,b]$: $\frac1{b-a}\int_a^bf$.
- **Riemann sum:** $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^nf\!\left(\frac kn\right)=\int_0^1f(x)dx$.
- Numerical: trapezoidal rule is exact for degree $\le1$; Simpson's $\tfrac13$ rule is exact for degree $\le3$.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Symmetric limits dikhein to pehle even/odd check karo. $|f|$ ke integral me sign change wale point par todo.

sections.title: Probability and Statistics — Probability, Conditional Probability and Bayes
sections.summary: Axioms, independence, conditional probability, total probability, Bayes' theorem.
sections.content:
## 1. Axioms and basic rules

$0\le P(A)\le1$, $P(S)=1$, additivity for mutually exclusive events.

$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B),\qquad P(A')=1-P(A)$$

$$P(A\cup B\cup C)=\sum P(A)-\sum P(A\cap B)+P(A\cap B\cap C)$$

Classical probability: $\dfrac{\text{favourable outcomes}}{\text{total equally likely outcomes}}$ (use $\binom nr$ for selections). "At least one" $=1-P(\text{none})$.

## 2. Conditional probability and independence

$$P(A|B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\qquad P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B|A)$$

- $A,B$ independent iff $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$ iff $P(A|B)=P(A)$. Then $A$ and $B'$ (and $A'$ and $B'$) are also independent.
- **Mutually exclusive** events with positive probability are **dependent** ($P(A\cap B)=0\ne P(A)P(B)$). Mutually exclusive and independent are different ideas.
- $P(A|B)\ne P(B|A)$ in general.

## 3. Total probability and Bayes' theorem

If $B_1,\dots,B_n$ partition the sample space:

$$P(A)=\sum_iP(A|B_i)P(B_i),\qquad P(B_i|A)=\frac{P(A|B_i)P(B_i)}{\sum_jP(A|B_j)P(B_j)}$$

**Medical test example:** prevalence 1%, sensitivity 99%, false-positive rate 5%:

$$P(D|+)=\frac{0.99\times0.01}{0.99\times0.01+0.05\times0.99}=\frac{0.0099}{0.0594}=\frac16\approx0.167$$

(Even a good test gives a modest posterior when the disease is rare: the base rate matters.)

## 4. Classic results

- Two dice: $P(\text{sum}=7)=\frac16$.
- Two children, at least one boy: $P(\text{both boys})=\frac13$.
- Drawing without replacement: use $\binom nr$ or multiply conditional probabilities.
- Birthday paradox: probability of a repeated birthday exceeds $\frac12$ for 23 people.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Bayes me pehle tree banao: har branch ka probability likho, phir "given" wale event ko denominator me rakho.

sections.title: Probability and Statistics — Random Variables
sections.summary: PMF, PDF, CDF, expectation, variance, covariance, Markov and Chebyshev inequalities.
sections.content:
## 1. PMF, PDF and CDF

- **Discrete:** PMF $p(x)=P(X=x)$, $p\ge0$, $\sum p(x)=1$.
- **Continuous:** PDF $f(x)\ge0$, $\int_{-\infty}^\infty f=1$, $P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^bf$. For any single value $P(X=a)=0$.
- **CDF:** $F(x)=P(X\le x)$. Non-decreasing, right continuous, $F(-\infty)=0$, $F(\infty)=1$. For continuous $X$: $f=F'$. $P(a<X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)$.

## 2. Expectation and variance

$$E[X]=\sum xp(x)\ \text{ or }\ \int xf(x)dx,\qquad E[g(X)]=\sum g(x)p(x)\ \text{ or }\ \int g(x)f(x)dx$$

$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2,\qquad \sigma=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}}$$

- $E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b$, $\ \operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$
- $E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]$ **always** (even if dependent)
- $\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}X+\operatorname{Var}Y+2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$
- $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]$
- Independent $\Rightarrow$ $E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]$ and $\operatorname{Cov}=0$ (uncorrelated). **Converse is false.**
- Median $m$ of a continuous variable: $F(m)=\frac12$.

## 3. Linearity with indicator variables

Write a count as a sum of indicators and add expectations. Example: the expected number of fixed points of a random permutation of $n$ items is $n\cdot\frac1n=1$.

## 4. Inequalities

- **Markov** ($X\ge0$, $a>0$): $P(X\ge a)\le\dfrac{E[X]}{a}$
- **Chebyshev:** $P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)\le\dfrac1{k^2}$, so $P(|X-\mu|<k\sigma)\ge1-\frac1{k^2}$

## 5. Joint distributions

Marginal: sum/integrate the joint over the other variable. Independent iff joint = product of marginals. Law of total expectation: $E[X]=E[E[X|Y]]$.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Constant $c$ nikalne ke liye total probability = 1 lagao. Variance hamesha $E[X^2]-E[X]^2$ se nikalo.

sections.title: Probability and Statistics — Mean, Median, Mode and Standard Deviation
sections.summary: Measures of central tendency and dispersion, effect of shifting and scaling, combined groups.
sections.content:
## 1. Central tendency

- **Mean** $\bar x=\frac1n\sum x_i$
- **Median:** middle value of sorted data (average of the two middle values if $n$ is even)
- **Mode:** most frequent value (may be non-unique or absent)
- Symmetric distribution: mean = median = mode (if unimodal).
- For moderately skewed data: $\text{Mode}\approx3\,\text{Median}-2\,\text{Mean}$ (i.e. mean − mode ≈ 3(mean − median)).
- Median is robust to outliers; mean is not.

## 2. Dispersion

- Range = max − min
- **Population variance** $\sigma^2=\frac1N\sum(x_i-\mu)^2=\frac1N\sum x_i^2-\mu^2$
- **Sample variance** $s^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$ (divide by $n-1$)
- Standard deviation = $\sqrt{\text{variance}}$
- Coefficient of variation $=\dfrac{\sigma}{\mu}\times100\%$
- For the first $n$ natural numbers: mean $\frac{n+1}2$, variance $\frac{n^2-1}{12}$.

## 3. Effect of transformations

For $y_i=ax_i+b$: $\ \bar y=a\bar x+b$, $\ \sigma_y=|a|\sigma_x$, $\ \sigma_y^2=a^2\sigma_x^2$.

Adding a constant shifts the mean but leaves variance and SD unchanged. Multiplying by $a$ multiplies SD by $|a|$.

## 4. Useful facts

- $\sum(x_i-\bar x)=0$.
- Mean minimizes $\sum(x_i-c)^2$; median minimizes $\sum|x_i-c|$.
- Combined mean of two groups: $\bar x=\dfrac{n_1\bar x_1+n_2\bar x_2}{n_1+n_2}$.
- Combined variance: $\sigma^2=\dfrac{n_1(\sigma_1^2+d_1^2)+n_2(\sigma_2^2+d_2^2)}{n_1+n_2}$ with $d_i=\bar x_i-\bar x$.
- Grouped data median: $L+\dfrac{N/2-F}{f}h$; mode: $L+\dfrac{f_1-f_0}{2f_1-f_0-f_2}h$.

**Worked example:** data $2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9$: mean 5, median 4.5, mode 4, population variance $\frac{9+1+1+1+0+0+4+16}{8}=4$, SD $=2$.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Pehle dekho population hai ya sample: sample me $n-1$ se divide hota hai. Shift se SD nahi badalta, scaling se badalta hai.

sections.title: Probability and Statistics — Uniform, Normal, Exponential, Poisson and Binomial
sections.summary: Formulas, mean/variance, memoryless property, normal tables, relations between distributions.
sections.content:
## 1. Summary table

| Distribution | PMF / PDF | Mean | Variance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bernoulli($p$) | $P(1)=p,\ P(0)=1-p$ | $p$ | $p(1-p)$ |
| Binomial($n,p$) | $\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ | $np$ | $np(1-p)$ |
| Poisson($\lambda$) | $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$ | $\lambda$ | $\lambda$ |
| Geometric($p$) (trials to first success) | $(1-p)^{k-1}p$ | $\frac1p$ | $\frac{1-p}{p^2}$ |
| Discrete uniform $1..n$ | $\frac1n$ | $\frac{n+1}2$ | $\frac{n^2-1}{12}$ |
| Uniform($a,b$) | $\frac1{b-a}$ on $[a,b]$ | $\frac{a+b}2$ | $\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}$ |
| Exponential($\lambda$) | $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, $x\ge0$ | $\frac1\lambda$ | $\frac1{\lambda^2}$ |
| Normal($\mu,\sigma^2$) | $\frac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma^2$ |

## 2. Binomial and Poisson

- Binomial: number of successes in $n$ independent trials. Sum of independent Binomial($n_i$,$p$) is Binomial($\sum n_i,p$). Mean $>$ variance.
- Poisson: counts of rare events; **mean = variance = $\lambda$**. Sum of independent Poissons is Poisson($\lambda_1+\lambda_2$). Binomial($n,p$) $\approx$ Poisson($np$) for large $n$, small $p$.
- Poisson process of rate $r$: number of events in time $t$ is Poisson($rt$); the waiting time between events is Exponential($r$).

## 3. Exponential and uniform

- CDF: $F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$, so $P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$.
- **Memoryless:** $P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)=e^{-\lambda t}$. The geometric distribution is the only memoryless discrete distribution.
- Minimum of independent Exp($\lambda_1$), Exp($\lambda_2$) is Exp($\lambda_1+\lambda_2$).
- Uniform: $P(c<X<d)=\frac{d-c}{b-a}$.

## 4. Normal distribution

- Bell-shaped, symmetric about $\mu$; mean = median = mode $=\mu$.
- Standardize: $Z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim N(0,1)$.
- $\Phi(0)=0.5$, $\Phi(1)=0.8413$, $\Phi(1.96)=0.975$, $\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)$.
- Empirical rule: $P(|Z|<1)=0.6827$, $P(|Z|<2)=0.9545$, $P(|Z|<3)=0.9973$.
- Linear combination of independent normals is normal: $aX+bY\sim N(a\mu_X+b\mu_Y,\ a^2\sigma_X^2+b^2\sigma_Y^2)$.
- Binomial($n,p$) $\approx N(np,\,np(1-p))$ for large $n$ (central limit theorem).

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Normal wale sawaal me pehle $Z$ me convert karo. Poisson me $\lambda$ time ke saath scale hota hai: 30 min ka $\lambda=$ rate $\times0.5$.
keyPoints: Sum of independent normals: means add, variances add
Poisson process: counts Poisson, gaps exponential
